query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

cited_evidence.text: W-based refractory HEAs (RHEAs) have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical strength at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys or pure W,. Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of knowledge on thermal stability at higher temperatures and irradiation resistance, which are important aspects to consider for the behavior of the materials subject to extreme environments, especially nuclear fusion. Refractory, low activation high-entropy alloys such as TiVCrTa [], TiVCrFeMn [], and (CrVTiTa)1−xWx [], where x is the atomic fraction (0.3 to 0.9), have been proposed for nuclear applications. This class of alloys is particularly promising as a thermal barrier interlayer due to its high thermal stability [] and high temperature strength [,], as well as high radiation resistance [] and low thermal diffusivity []. Granberg et al. () combined experiments and modeling to identify the sluggish mobility of dislocation loops as the main mechanism leading to radiation tolerance in Ni-based FCC HEAs. Kumar et al. () showed how Ni-based FCC HEAs lead to less radiation-induced segregation and fewer voids, although hardness was observed to increase after irradiation. Other studies show results in the same direction, with HEAs improving radiation tolerance in both FCC and BCC structures (). Very recently, W-based quinary HEAs with diverse composition have been synthesized as potential materials for fusion applications. The authors observed the formation of Ti carbides and laves phases at large W concentrations. The authors studied the mechanical response, showing that these materials could lead to twofold improvement in the hardness and strength due to solid solution strengthening and dispersion strengthening (). However, refractory HEAs have never been tested under irradiation for potential uses as PFMs or structural materials in nuclear fusion environments. decision.trend: Research has been focused on developing high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with improved properties such as irradiation resistance, mechanical durability, and thermal conductivity. Studies have shown that HEAs can exhibit enhanced properties due to their unique microstructure and composition. The trend is to design and optimize HEAs for specific applications, including nuclear and aerospace industries.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to balance the trade-offs between different properties, such as thermal conductivity, mechanical durability, and irradiation resistance, in HEAs. Additionally, the effects of various processing routes and conditions on the microstructure and properties of HEAs need to be further understood and optimized.
decision.why: The addition of refractory elements, such as W, Ta, and Hf, has been shown to improve the thermal stability and radiation resistance of HEAs. This approach could be explored to increase the thermal conductivity of W-Cu metal-matrix composites while retaining their mechanical durability and irradiation resistance.
